pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Physical vs Chemical Changes

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry & Physics 'Matter'):** Chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms; the difference between chemical and physical changes; conservation of mass in changes of state and chemical reactions.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-2):** Analyse [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-2] they interact to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred.

- **Operational details:** The dividing line: a PHYSICAL change alters form or state but makes NO new substance and is usually reversible (melting, dissolving, shaping) — the same particles, just rearranged in space; a CHEMICAL change REARRANGES ATOMS into new substances with different properties, usually hard to reverse (burning, rusting, cooking). The particle-level story is the key upgrade from KS2's observational reversible/irreversible work: in a physical change existing molecules stay intact and only move; in a chemical change bonds break and new bonds form, so the atoms regroup into different molecules. Diagnose a chemical change by evidence (new substance signalled by colour change, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after (MS-PS1-2). Conservation of mass holds in BOTH (atoms are neither created nor destroyed). Guard the overlap with reversible/irreversible: not all physical changes are trivially reversible in practice, but none make new substances.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B–C (early-formal). The child classifies a change as physical or chemical using property-change evidence and the atom-rearrangement idea, and explains that mass is conserved in both because atoms are only regrouped.
bestPractices: Define the split at the particle level: physical = intact molecules rearranged; chemical = bonds break and atoms regroup into new substances.
Diagnose chemical change by evidence (new substance: colour, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after.
Stress conservation of mass in BOTH change types — atoms are only rearranged.
Use ambiguous cases (dissolving = physical) to sharpen the 'no new substance' criterion.
Connect to KS2 reversible/irreversible while upgrading it with the atom-rearrangement mechanism.
keyRepresentations: A macro event synced to a particle window (molecules intact vs atoms regrouping)
A conserved-mass balance readout across the change
commonMisconceptions: A change is chemical whenever the appearance changes (colour, state).
Mass changes during a chemical reaction (atoms created or destroyed).
Dissolving is a chemical change because the solid 'disappears'.
Physical changes are always easily reversible and chemical ones never.
New atoms are created in a reaction, rather than existing atoms being regrouped.

learn.summary: Learners distinguish physical from chemical changes using a particle-level criterion — in a physical change existing particles stay intact and only rearrange in space; in a chemical change bonds break and atoms regroup into new substances. They diagnose chemical change by observable evidence (colour change, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after, and they explain that mass is conserved in BOTH types because atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed — provided all atoms involved (including any gas taken from or released to the surroundings) are counted. Ambiguous cases (dissolving, melting) sharpen the 'no new substance' rule against a weaker 'reversibility' or 'appearance' test.

activities.title: Change classifier: macro stage synced to a particle window
feedback: If a learner labels dissolving chemical because the solid disappeared, point to the particle window: the same particles dispersed among the water particles and can be recovered by evaporation — no new substance formed, so the change is physical.

If a learner expects mass to change in the burning case, return to the particle window and count atoms before and after: the magnesium combines with oxygen from the air, and every atom (magnesium and oxygen) is still present, just regrouped, so the total mass of the closed system is conserved — on an open bench balance the collected solid product is heavier than the original magnesium (if none escapes as smoke) precisely because it has gained that oxygen.
If a learner relies on 'reversible vs irreversible', note that this often correlates but is not the definition; the robust test is whether a new substance formed.

Confirm correct reasoning by having the learner name what the particle view showed: intact particles of the same substance rearranging (physical) versus bonds breaking and new substances forming (chemical).
activities.rationale: The physical/chemical distinction is defined at the particle level, and the key KS3 upgrade from observational reversible/irreversible work is the atom-rearrangement mechanism. A synced macro-and-particle view with a property comparator and a mass readout makes the defining feature — whether the substance stays the same or atoms regroup — directly observable, and the dissolving case targets the common 'looks different so it's chemical' error.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3: chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms; difference between chemical and physical changes; conservation of mass
Students judge change type by appearance and think mass changes in reactions; the atom-rearrangement view and property comparison correct this
learnerActions: Trigger melting wax: observe the macro stage turn liquid, and in the particle window watch the same wax molecules loosen and slide while staying whole.
Check the before/after property panel ('same substance') and the mass-balance readout; label the change physical.

Trigger burning magnesium: observe the macro stage flare white, and in the particle window watch magnesium atoms combine with oxygen atoms drawn from the surrounding air into a new white compound (magnesium oxide).

Check the property panel ('new substance, new properties') and confirm that when every atom — including the oxygen taken from the air — is counted, the closed-system mass balance still holds; note that on an open bench balance the solid product would weigh more than the original magnesium, provided all of the product is collected, because it has gained that oxygen; label the change chemical.

Classify a dissolving case: observe the solid seem to disappear on the macro stage while the particle window shows the same particles dispersing among the water particles, not new substances forming; label it physical despite the changed appearance.
For each case, state the rule you used: did the particles stay as the same substance (physical) or did atoms regroup into new substances (chemical)?
activities.intendedInsight: The only difference that matters is whether the substance's particles stayed the same or atoms regrouped into new substances; mass is conserved either way because atoms are only rearranged (counting every atom involved, including any gas exchanged with the surroundings). A changed appearance (state, colour, a solid 'disappearing') is not by itself evidence of a chemical change.

activities.title: Predict-Observe-Explain: dissolving versus displacement
feedback: If a learner predicts dissolving makes a new substance, note that a solution is a recoverable mixture — the solid can be recovered by evaporation unchanged, so no new substance formed.

If a learner says mass changes in a sealed reaction, re-anchor on atom conservation: in a sealed flask no atoms enter or leave, so the same atoms are present before and after and total mass is unchanged.
For baking a cake, accept evidence-based answers that cite new substances (gas from raising agents, browning, irreversible texture) as signs of chemical change, rather than a reversibility claim.
activities.rationale: Predict-Observe-Explain makes the learner commit to a rule before seeing the result, surfacing reliance on appearance or reversibility. Contrasting dissolving (physical) with a displacement reaction (chemical) targets an appearance-based classifier, which may wrongly call dissolving chemical. A reversibility rule happens to classify both correctly, so reliance on it is revealed only through the learner's stated explanations.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-PS1-2: analyse and interpret data on properties before and after interaction to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred
Students judge change type by appearance and think mass changes in reactions; the atom-rearrangement view and property comparison correct this
learnerActions: Before observing, predict for adding blue (hydrated) copper sulfate crystals to warm water whether a NEW substance will form, and explain why.
Before observing, predict for dropping an iron nail into copper sulfate solution whether a NEW substance will form, and explain why.

Observe both: the blue copper sulfate crystals dissolve (blue solution, crystals recoverable by gentle evaporation/crystallisation, no new substance); the iron nail turns copper-coloured and the blue fades (a new substance forms).
Compare each prediction with what happened, and revise any rule that relied on reversibility or appearance rather than 'was a new substance made?'.

Answer probes: why is dissolving sugar physical but rusting chemical? What signs show a new substance has formed? Does total mass change in a sealed flask, and why not? Is baking a cake physical or chemical, and what is your evidence?
activities.intendedInsight: Pre-observation reasoning exposes whether a learner classifies by 'new substance formed?' or by a weaker reversibility/appearance test. The dissolving case is the key discriminator: its dramatic appearance change tempts an appearance-based classifier to call it chemical even though no new substance forms, whereas the displacement reaction genuinely is chemical — so committing to a rule before observing reveals which criterion the learner is actually using.

activities.title: Classify and justify the rule
feedback: If the learner classifies solely by reversibility and stumbles on reversible chemical changes or hard-to-reverse physical ones, shift the criterion to 'new substance made?' and show a reversible chemical change alongside an awkward-to-reverse physical one.
If dissolving is placed in the chemical pile, note that dissolving makes a recoverable mixture; the sugar is unchanged, so no new substance → physical.
If melting or boiling is called chemical, use the particle picture to show the same particles rearrange — still the same substance.
Credit full reasoning only when the rule is 'new substance made?', signs are named, and mass conservation is justified by atoms being regrouped.
activities.rationale: Asking for the rule, not just the sort, is the discriminator: all three sorted items (melting, dissolving, rusting) are classified the same way by a reversibility rule and a new-substance rule, so the sort alone cannot tell the two apart. Only cases such as reversible chemical changes or hard-to-reverse physical changes separate them, so requiring the stated rule, plus such follow-up cases, reveals which criterion the learner holds. This is a check/assessment activity best paired after the exploratory sim.
sourceClaims: NGSS MS-PS1-2: analyse and interpret data on properties before and after interaction to determine whether a chemical reaction has occurred
learnerActions: Sort three changes into physical and chemical: (a) ice melting to water, (b) sugar dissolving in tea, (c) a nail rusting.
State the RULE used — what has to happen for a change to count as chemical.
Interpret before/after property data for further cases to decide whether a chemical reaction occurred.
For a chemical change occurring in a sealed flask, state whether total mass changes and justify using atom conservation.
activities.intendedInsight: A robust classifier rests on 'was a new substance made?' (often signalled by colour change, gas, temperature change, or precipitate, though these signs alone are not proof, since boiling releases gas and some dissolving changes temperature or colour), not on 'is it reversible?'. State changes and dissolving stay physical because the same substance is preserved, and mass is conserved in chemical changes because atoms are only regrouped.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal contrast panel (consolidation)
feedback: Prompt the learner to say explicitly whether any new substance appears in the 'after' picture; if none does, the change is physical.
If a learner conflates a state change with a new substance, point to identical particles in both pictures.
activities.rationale: A reveal-and-describe panel consolidates the vocabulary and the particle contrast. It is a scaffold: fixed pictures support recognition and verbalisation but do not let the learner trigger changes, watch bonds break and reform, or test their own classifications, so it complements rather than replaces the interactive sim.
learnerActions: Reveal paired before/after particle pictures for a physical change (same particles, rearranged) and a chemical change (bonds broken, new substances formed).
Describe in your own words what stayed the same and what changed at the particle level for each.
Match each revealed example to the evidence that signals a new substance (or its absence).
activities.intendedInsight: Static particle pictures let learners rehearse and verbalise the same-substance-versus-regrouped-atoms contrast and connect it to observable evidence.

constraints: Define the split at the particle level: physical = same substance's particles rearranged; chemical = bonds break and atoms regroup into new substances.
Diagnose chemical change by evidence (new substance: colour, gas, heat/light, precipitate) AND by comparing properties before and after.

Stress conservation of mass in BOTH change types — atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed; when a gas is exchanged with the surroundings (e.g. magnesium gaining oxygen from the air), it must be counted, so an open bench balance can still show a change in the mass of the solid.
Use ambiguous cases (dissolving, melting) to sharpen the 'no new substance' criterion against reversibility- or appearance-based tests.
Connect to KS2 reversible/irreversible while upgrading it with the atom-rearrangement mechanism; note that not all physical changes are trivially reversible in practice, but none make new substances.

The tap-to-reveal contrast panel is a recognition/verbalisation scaffold: it does not let learners trigger changes or test classifications, so it supports but does not substitute for the interactive investigation.

A classification task with fixed response options checks sorting and data interpretation but does not by itself elicit the learner's independently generated rule or reasoning; pair it with a task that asks for the justification.

Mass-conservation and property examples (wax melting, magnesium burning, iron/copper sulfate displacement) depend on the specified setup; present them as the stated scenarios rather than universal outcomes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source labelled a 2D interactive 'ideal' and rated 3D and conversation 'poor' as catalog fit judgements. These are framed here as fit-for-purpose proposals: a 2D particle view suits a particle-rearrangement concept, but this does not establish that 3D or dialogue 'add nothing' or 'cannot teach' the idea. The comparative-efficacy framing in the original has been softened.

The original claim that a static image 'cannot animate bonds breaking/forming or let the child test and classify' is retained only as a scope note (the panel supports recognition/verbalisation), not as a universal 'static art cannot teach' law.
Two of three sources are marked verified:false in the row (NGSS MS-PS1-2 and the BEST diagnostics claim); evidence strength has not been upgraded here.

The POE displacement example (iron nail in copper sulfate) and magnesium burning involve reagents that require appropriate supervision/safety in a real classroom; the row does not specify safety handling.

Magnesium burning is the classic case where an open-air demonstration shows the solid gaining mass; conservation of total mass only holds literally when the oxygen taken from the air is included. The activity now states this explicitly rather than implying no mass change.

Dissolving copper sulfate (the POE physical example) separates the ionic solid into ions in solution rather than keeping intact molecules; it is still a physical change by the recovery/no-new-substance test, but the generic 'particles disperse' wording is preferred over 'molecules stay intact' for ionic solutes.

In this POE pair a strict reversibility classifier happens to label both cases correctly; it is specifically the appearance-based classifier that mislabels dissolving, which is why the activity frames the dissolving case as the discriminator.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: add a spatula of copper sulfate to warm water (dissolves — physical) and, separately, drop an iron nail into copper sulfate solution (displacement — chemical, nail goes copper-coloured, blue fades). Ask the child to predict, for each, whether a NEW substance forms and WHY, before observing. A 'reversibility/appearance' classifier predicts wrongly. The pre-observation reasoning is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: Sugar dissolving looks permanent-ish and rusting looks permanent — so why is one physical and one chemical?
Name the signs you'd look for that tell you a NEW substance has formed.
A chemical reaction happens in a sealed flask — does the total mass change? Why not?
Is baking a cake physical or chemical? What's your evidence?
assess.correctAnswer: Physical: melting ice and dissolving sugar (no new substance — same stuff rearranged, reversible). Chemical: rusting (a NEW substance, iron oxide, forms). The rule: a CHEMICAL change makes one or more NEW substances (signalled by colour change, gas, temperature change, or a precipitate); a physical change makes none. Full marks rest the rule on 'new substance made?', not on 'is it reversible?'.

errorPatterns.pattern: reversibility is the whole test ('if you can undo it, it's physical; if you can't, it's chemical')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Shift the criterion to 'new substance made?'. Reversibility often correlates but isn't the definition — show a reversible chemical change and an awkward-to-reverse physical one.
errorPatterns.distractor: Rusting is chemical only because you can't undo it, and the others are physical because you can.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: classifies solely by whether it can be reversed; stumbles on reversible chemical changes or hard-to-reverse physical ones

errorPatterns.pattern: dissolving is a chemical change because 'the sugar reacts with the water / turns into something new'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Dissolving makes a mixture, recoverable by evaporation; the sugar is unchanged. No new substance → physical. Reconnect to conservation and recovery.
errorPatterns.distractor: Dissolving is chemical, because the sugar turns into a new substance in the tea.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: puts dissolving in the chemical pile, treating the solution as a new substance

errorPatterns.pattern: a change of state (melting/boiling) is chemical because 'it turned into something different'
errorPatterns.nextMove: State changes rearrange the SAME particles — still water, no new substance. Use the particle picture to show identity is preserved.
errorPatterns.distractor: Melting is chemical, because a solid turning into a liquid is a new substance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: labels melting/boiling chemical because the appearance/state changed

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by reversibility alone or by appearance; mislabels dissolving or melting as chemical; no 'new substance' criterion.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by whether a new substance formed, names the observable signs, keeps state changes and dissolving as physical using the particle/recovery argument, and explains mass is conserved in a chemical change — transferring to novel cases (baking, reversible reactions).
responseLevels.partial: Sorts the three correctly and states 'new substance = chemical', but leans on reversibility as backup and can't handle a reversible chemical change or justify via conservation of mass — rule stated, not yet robust.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are three changes: (a) ice melting to water, (b) sugar dissolving in tea, (c) a nail rusting. Sort them into 'physical change' and 'chemical change'. Then the important part: explain the RULE you used — what has to happen for a change to count as chemical?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two rule separates a child who classifies by 'was a new substance formed' from one who uses 'reversible = physical' as the whole test. Dissolving (reversible, physical) fits both rules, but rusting isn't easily reversed AND some chemical changes seem reversible — so only the 'new substance' rule classifies robustly. Asking for the rule, not just the sort, is the discriminator.
